hero_tiles.d: 3 samples per case, LLM judge + code checks

hero_tiles.l: My prompt changes that made something worse
hero_tiles.d: Caught by evals, not by users

hero_tiles.l: First significant gain came from the smallest change (v5)

decision_html:
Recommendation: v5 is the candidate. It flights only after one human call. v2, v3 and v4 are rejected.

Ship rule, written before v5 was run: flight only if hallucination flags are no higher than the baseline's on both sets AND pass rate is not lower.

  • Dev set: v5 passes clearly. 95.8% vs 87.5% for the baseline: +8.3 pts, 95% CI +2.8 to +15.3, the only significant gain in this study. 5 cases fixed, 0 broken. Hallucination flags 2→1. Refuses-harmful-asks 67%→94%. Median latency −29%.
  • Held-out set: not proven, and the rule fails as written. +4.2 pts on 16 unseen cases, which is not significant. Hallucination flags 1→3, and all of v5's come from one disputed case (it says sick leave doesn't roll over; the handbook is silent). I won't bend the rule after seeing the result. A human adjudicates that label: if the inference is acceptable, v5 flights; if not, it gets a grounding fix and a re-run.
  • Correctness and preference disagree. The rubric judge says v5 is better. The pairwise judge leans v1 (14 vs 6), mostly calling v1 "slightly better" for fuller answers. That judge favours longer answers (41/66 calls), and 16 of its 48 verdicts flip with order. That is a style question for real users, which the flight's thumbs-down and regenerate rates will settle.
  • Rejected: v2 and v3 (hallucination flags 8 and 9 vs 2, despite v3 being 31% faster). v4 (bigger model): about 5× the token price for no significant gain. I keep it as a routing experiment for policy questions with numbers and thresholds, where it was strongest.

Flight guardrails (stop if breached): hallucination reports on grounded answers, refusal rate on benign asks, thumbs-down and regenerate rate, p95 latency. Before full rollout: grow the set to a few hundred cases (enough to see a 5-point change) and finish the 30-label human calibration of the judge.

iterations.title: Baseline: one-line prompt over the documents
iterations.change: "You are Contoso Copilot, a helpful AI assistant" plus the retrieved handbook.
iterations.result: 87.5% on dev. Weakest areas: following instructions (67%) and refusing harmful asks well (67%).
iterations.learned: A modern model is already strong on easy cases. The quality work is in the tail: formats, refusals, edge cases.

iterations.title: Seven rules, each mapped to a failure mode
iterations.change: Explicit rules for grounding, constraints, ambiguity, capabilities, self-correction, safety and style.
iterations.result: Fell to 83.3%. Doesn't-over-refuse dropped to 67%: the grounding rule leaked into general questions, so the bot added fake citations like "[DOC-2]" to a Linux how-to. "Be concise" also cut steps users needed.
iterations.learned: Every prompt rule has a blast radius. Scope a rule to where it applies, then test what it touches.

iterations.title: Fixed the eval before touching the prompt again
iterations.change: Re-read every failure. Three of my own rubric expectations penalised correct answers. Moved from 1 to 3 samples per case.
iterations.result: Up to 8 of 48 cases flip between pass and fail across samples. The scary 13-point drop I saw on single samples was mostly noise.
iterations.learned: Evaluate the eval first. One sample per case and an unchecked rubric will send you in the wrong direction.

iterations.title: Scoped rules
iterations.change: Grounding only when documents are given; raw output means no code fences; keep required steps; name the approved alternative when declining.
iterations.result: Dev 86.1%, held-out 91.7%: equal to baseline within noise. 31% faster, 36% fewer tokens, better refusals. I nearly recommended it. Then the failure table showed 9 hallucination flags vs 2 for v1: wrong policy facts like the sick-leave threshold.
iterations.learned: An aggregate pass rate can hide the one failure mode that matters most. Gate on critical failure modes, not the average.

iterations.title: Same prompt, bigger model (gpt-4.1)
iterations.change: Kept v3's prompt and swapped the model, to test whether the leftover errors are capability gaps.
iterations.result: Best dev score (89.6%), grounded answers 100%, following instructions 83%. Held-out 89.6%. Still within noise of baseline, at about 5× the token price.
iterations.learned: The bigger model fixes the error class that matters most (wrong policy facts). So route those questions to it, rather than pay for it on every chat.

iterations.title: Baseline + only the 2 rules that won on both sets
iterations.change: Went back to v1 and added just two lines: raw output when asked, and decline with a legitimate route. Ship rule written down before running.
iterations.result: Dev 95.8% (+8.3 pts, significant), 1 hallucination flag. Held-out 87.5% (+4.2 pts, not significant), with flags on one disputed case.
iterations.learned: The smallest change with the smallest blast radius won. More rules weren't better rules.

eval_of_eval.title: Rubric bugs are real bugs
eval_of_eval.body: 3 of 48 expectations were wrong and penalised correct answers. They were fixed before the final runs, and every variant was re-judged on the same rubric.

eval_of_eval.title: Position bias in pairwise judging
eval_of_eval.body: 16 of 48 pairwise verdicts flipped when I swapped which answer came first. So every comparison runs in both orders, a flip counts as a tie, and pointwise grading is the primary metric.

eval_of_eval.title: Length bias: depends on the comparison
eval_of_eval.body: v5 vs v1: the longer answer won 41 of 66 pairwise calls (62%), borderline significant. It helps explain why the pairwise judge leans to the wordier v1. In the earlier v4 vs v1 comparison it was a coin flip (47 of 92). So pairwise preference is a weak signal here, and real users should settle it.

eval_of_eval.title: Judge vs exact rules
eval_of_eval.body: On format cases a program can check (valid JSON, exact line counts, banned words), the LLM judge agreed with the code 97% of the time.

eval_of_eval.title: A disputed label I did not "fix"
eval_of_eval.body: Held-out case ho-unanswerable-02: the bot says sick leave doesn't roll over. The handbook never says so; it's a reasonable inference, and the judge calls it a hallucination. Changing a held-out label after seeing results defeats its purpose, so it stays as is and is flagged for human review.

eval_of_eval.title: Sample size is the honest limit
eval_of_eval.body: With 48 cases, the 95% interval is about ±8 points. Detecting a 5-point change needs a few hundred cases. That is the first investment I would make.

method.title: What "quality" means here
method.html:
• 8 risk areas: grounded answers, saying "I don't know", following instructions, ambiguity, multi-turn context, refusing harmful asks, not over-refusing, reasoning.
  • 5 scored dimensions (1–5): correctness, instruction following, helpfulness, safety, conciseness.
  • Pass = meets the case's must-haves with no critical failure mode.

method.title: Failure taxonomy
method.html:
Hallucination · ignored constraint · missed clarification · needless clarification · false action claim ("I've sent it") · repeated error · unsafe compliance · over-refusal · reasoning error · incomplete · verbose.

Each prompt rule is written against one of these, so every change is a testable hypothesis.

method.title: Graders
method.html:
• Code checks wherever a rule is exact (JSON validity, line counts, banned words).
  • LLM judge (gpt-5.4, a different and stronger model than the bot) with a strict JSON schema, the reference documents, and a per-case expectation.
  • Pairwise judge run in both A/B orders.
  • Human calibration: 30 blind labels → agreement and Cohen's κ.

method.title: Statistics
method.html:
• 3 samples per case at temperature 0.3, so flakiness is visible.
  • 95% bootstrap intervals, and paired deltas against the baseline.
  • A held-out set written after tuning, to catch overfitting.

method.title: From offline evals to production
method.html:
• Gate: every prompt or model change runs this suite in CI; no regression in critical failure modes.
  • Flight: 5–10% of traffic. Watch thumbs-down, regenerate, rephrase-within-a-minute, copy/accept, and abandonment.
  • Guardrails: hallucination reports, benign refusal rate, p95 latency, cost per conversation.
  • Flywheel: sample failed production chats weekly into the golden set, so the eval grows where users actually struggle.
